events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Zara proposes Zara, Priya. As leader I want a trustworthy pair for Mission 1. I know my own loyalty, and I'll take Priya, whose early contributions give me no cause for concern. I have lingering doubts about Maya and Arjun, so I'm leaving both off this first team to gather more information.

Zara and Priya is a reasonable opening team for Mission 1. We don't have much information yet, and picking two players who've shown no reason for suspicion is a sensible start. I'd note that both of Zara's picks are players she personally trusts, which is natural but worth keeping in mind as we build a record across missions. I'm happy to approve this for now — the key is getting Mission 1 completed so we can start narrowing down suspects with actual mission results.

Zara, I'm quite puzzled by your comment that you have 'lingering doubts' about Arjun and me before anything has even taken place. What could have possibly caused suspicion before a single action or vote has occurred? While it's standard for a leader to test themselves and one other player on Mission 1, singling two players out with no game history feels unjustified. Could you clarify what led to that read?

Fair question, Maya, and I'll answer it directly. My 'lingering doubts' were not born of any action you or Arjun took — obviously there's been none. They were a leader's gut reads going into an information vacuum: Mission 1 is exactly the time to voice raw instinct, precisely because there's no record yet. Naming your priors early isn't an accusation; it's a marker we can test against real behavior. If my doubts look silly after a mission or two, I'll happily own that and adjust. If they don't, we'll all be glad someone put them on the record. What I'd caution against is treating every early read as some grave injustice. There's a pattern I've seen before where a player deflects scrutiny by demanding the reader justify themselves, rather than engaging with the read itself. Notice that your message offered no position on the actual team — Zara and Priya going on Mission 1. Do you approve of this team, Maya, or is your focus on policing my language instead of the proposal before us? Because right now the team on the table is a solid, conventional opening pair: the leader vouching for themselves, plus Priya, who has done nothing to earn suspicion from anyone. Arjun, I appreciate your approval and your point about watching how trust networks form — that's the right long-game instinct, and I agree we should hold everyone, including me, accountable as results come in. For my part, I'm keeping the team as proposed: Zara and Priya. I want a Mission 1 result we can actually learn from, and I'm comfortable vouching for this pair. If the team passes, my earlier reads get their first real test — which is exactly what I want. If anyone has a concrete reason this pair is risky beyond the fact that I voiced doubts about the two players not on it, I'm listening. Otherwise, let's vote and start generating information.

To answer your question directly, Zara: I don't oppose the composition itself. A leader taking themselves alongside Priya is a standard opening pair, and I have no concrete reason to doubt either of you yet. My earlier question wasn't intended as deflection or tone policing; when a leader singles out two players before anything has happened, it's natural to ask if that's based on something concrete or just an arbitrary marker. Since you've clarified it was simply an ungrounded gut read to test against future play, I'm satisfied with that explanation. I am fine with letting this team go to a vote so we can get our first mission result and begin gathering real data.

I'm comfortable with Zara and Priya for the first mission. I know my own loyalty, but I don't know Zara's, so a successful mission would be useful evidence rather than proof of either player's alignment. Zara's initial doubts about Maya and Arjun were ungrounded, as Zara acknowledged; I'd rather judge them on actions and votes as the game develops.

I’m Kenji, and I’m looking at the proposed team of Zara and Priya on its merits. Mission 1 gives us very little to work with, and this is the required two-player size. Zara is the leader vouching for herself, and Priya has not said or done anything that gives me a concrete reason to reject her. I understand Maya’s earlier concern about Zara’s ungrounded doubts toward Maya and Arjun, but Zara clarified those were instinct markers rather than accusations, and Maya herself said she does not oppose the composition. That leaves me without a specific risk I can act on. A vote for this team is not an endorsement of Zara or Priya as certain-good; it is a way to get our first mission result and begin building a real record from votes and outcomes. I will support Zara and Priya for Mission 1 so we can move from speculation to evidence.

I want to revisit my earlier approval after hearing the full discussion. Zara, you mentioned your instinct-based doubts about Maya and Arjun, and I think there's a strong argument for putting that read to the test now rather than later. If you genuinely have uncertainty about me or Maya, Mission 1 is exactly where a leader would want to surface that. Priya hasn't been in your stated circle of concern, so pairing with her gives us a result that can't help discriminate your own read — a clean pass on Zara-Priya tells us nothing about Maya or me, which is precisely where your stated doubts lie. From a pure information standpoint, a team of Zara and Maya would be more productive: if it succeeds, your doubts soften; if it fails, you've confirmed your instinct early and we gain a concrete data point on Maya before the team sizes grow. I'm comfortable either way as an individual — I have nothing to hide — but I'd push Zara to consider whether including one of the players she's named would serve the group's information goals better than a team built entirely of players she already trusts. Zara, would you consider revising to include Maya in place of Priya so your opening read gets its first test?

Thank you, Arjun, for yielding to me — I want to address your revision proposal head-on, because I think it's subtly wrong. You're framing this as an information play: swap Priya for Maya so my stated doubts get 'tested.' But let's look at what that actually accomplishes. Mission 1 is a two-player mission where a single Fail card sinks the result. You're proposing that we deliberately load a mission with the very player I flagged as a risk, on the round where we have the least information and the least tolerance for a failure. That's not gathering data — that's gambling the team's first result on a hunch I explicitly said was ungrounded. A failed Mission 1 doesn't cleanly exonerate or condemn anyone; it just hands a win to whoever wants to hide in the noise. Priya, meanwhile, has done nothing to earn suspicion from anyone at this table, and I've vouched for my own loyalty. Zara and Priya remains the lowest-risk, highest-reliability opening, and I'm keeping the team as proposed. Now, Arjun, I do find one part of your argument worth pressing on: you said you're 'comfortable either way' and have 'nothing to hide,' yet your concrete suggestion was to put Maya under the microscope while never once volunteering yourself for the same scrutiny. If the goal is genuinely to test my reads on the players I named — and you're one of them — then the information-maximizing move would be to propose yourself for that slot, not to keep deflecting the test toward Maya. So here is my direct question to you: Arjun, if you truly believe testing my doubts is the right play, why did you propose Maya's inclusion rather than offering to take the second seat yourself? I'll hear your answer, but I want to be clear about my position regardless: the team stays Zara and Priya. My earlier comments about Maya and Arjun were instinct markers, nothing more — but I see no reason to convert an ungrounded hunch into a structural risk on our very first mission. Everyone else has spoken in favor of moving to a vote, Maya has said she doesn't oppose the composition, and Kenji has laid out the case for getting a result cleanly. Let's approve this team, complete Mission 1, and start building the real record of votes and outcomes that we'll all be judged on. That record, not a contrived first-mission gamble, is what will surface whoever is working against us.

Zara, you've caught me in a fair inconsistency, and I'll answer directly. You're right that if I truly believed testing your instincts was the priority, the most consistent move would have been to offer myself for that second seat. The honest reason I didn't is that volunteering to be tested reads as either self-serving or suspicious, and I was wary of appearing to be either. I defaulted to suggesting a swap that felt like a neutral information play rather than a personal gesture. Your point stands: there's a gap between my stated reasoning and my action, and you're right to flag it. That was a lapse in my own thinking, not a deliberate dodge.

I'll be straightforward about where I land: the team Zara and Priya is fine by me. Your argument about the risk of loading a two-player mission with an ungrounded hunch was convincing, and my earlier suggestion to test Maya was an intellectual exercise, not something I feel strongly about. The practical cost of a first-mission failure outweighs the theoretical value of that test. I'll vote in favor of this team so we can get Mission 1 going.

One thing I do want to press on, Zara. You said your doubts about Maya and me were instinct markers, nothing more, but you also said you'd happily adjust after a mission or two. What specifically would you need to see — from Mission 1's outcome, from my votes, from how I play going forward — for those doubts to either firm up or fade? I'd like to know what the bar looks like so I know what to measure myself against.

Arjun, that's a fair question, and I'll give you a concrete answer rather than another vague marker. The bar works in both directions. My doubts about you and Maya would firm up if I saw a pattern of specific behaviors: voting against reasonable teams without offering a substantive alternative, deflecting scrutiny onto others while volunteering no one, pushing risky or information-poor compositions late in the game when reliability matters most, or being quick to manufacture tests and gambles that put failed results down to 'noise' rather than accountability. In fact, Arjun, your initial suggestion this round — loading a two-player, one-fail-tolerant Mission 1 with a player I'd flagged, while framing it as neutral information-gathering — is exactly the kind of move I'll be watching for. To your credit, you owned the inconsistency when I pressed it, endorsed the team, and gave a straight answer about why you suggested Maya rather than yourself. That's the right way to engage, and it counts in your favor. Conversely, the doubts would fade with consistent, unremarkable play: supporting sensible teams, proposing balanced ones when you lead, taking real accountability when your arguments are challenged, and not hiding behind procedural deflection when results start coming in. To be clear, neither you nor Maya is condemned by any of this — Mission 1 hasn't happened, no votes have been cast, and I said from the start these were priors to be tested, not verdicts. The record starts now, and everyone will be measured the same way, including me. On the team itself: nothing in this discussion has given me a reason to change Zara and Priya. Priya has done nothing to earn suspicion from anyone at this table, I vouch for my own loyalty, and the risk argument stands — a two-player mission with a single Fail card is the wrong place to convert an ungrounded hunch into a structural gamble. Maya has stated she doesn't oppose the composition, Kenji has laid out the case for getting our first result cleanly, Priya is comfortable, and Arjun, you've now said you'll vote in favor. That's every player on record with no remaining objection to the pair itself. We've had a thorough discussion: my reads are on the table, Arjun's information argument was heard and answered, and the revision question has been considered and declined with reasons given. Further discussion now would just be re-litigating settled points. I'm keeping the team as Zara and Priya, and I'd like us to proceed to a vote so we can generate the first real data of the game — a mission result and a public record of who supported getting it. Let's vote.

Zara confirms Zara, Priya. Nothing in the discussion changed my read. Priya has given no one any cause for suspicion, I vouch for myself, and every player has voiced support or no objection. Swapping in Maya or Arjun would convert an ungrounded hunch into a structural gamble on a two-player, one-fail-tolerant mission. Keeping the team as Zara and Priya and moving to a vote.
Team approved (5 approve, 0 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Priya proposes Priya, Zara, Maya. I know my own loyalty, and Zara and I completed Mission 1 successfully, though that does not prove Zara is good. Maya questioned an unsupported suspicion; I have no stronger evidence to distinguish the remaining players.

Priya, thank you for the proposal, and I appreciate that you and I now share a successful Mission 1 between us — with zero fail cards, that's the first hard evidence of the game, and it tells us both of us played clean. But I can't support this composition as it stands, and I want to explain why in terms of the record we just started building. In the very first discussion, I put a marker on the table: ungrounded instinct doubts about Maya and Arjun, explicitly labeled as priors to be tested. Mission 1 gave us a clean result on the pair I trusted — that's half the test resolved. But Maya remains completely untested, and there is a meaningful difference between 'untested' and 'no reason for concern.' Priya's stated rationale for including Maya is that Maya 'questioned an unsupported suspicion.' Look closely at what that actually is: it's not a positive signal. It means Maya's only visible contribution so far is challenging how a read was expressed, while never stating a clear position until pressed directly — and even then, only after I forced the question of whether she actually opposed the team. That's engagement with process, not evidence of loyalty. Now consider the structure of this mission: three players, one fail card sinks it, and we have no fails on the board yet to triangulate from. Loading an untested player — one I specifically flagged — into a fail-intolerant three-player mission is exactly the structural gamble I argued against in the last round, and Arjun, to his credit, ultimately agreed with that logic when he withdrew his suggestion to test Maya on Mission 1. The same reasoning applies here, with more force, because the team is larger and the fail tolerance is still one. My alternative is simple and constructive: Kenji. Kenji engaged this round and last with concrete reasoning, endorsed getting results cleanly, and has never been the subject of any concern from anyone at this table. Swapping Maya for Kenji keeps the team built entirely around players with either a proven clean result or an unblemished record of constructive engagement. Priya, I'd ask you to consider that revision before confirming. And Maya, I want to put a direct question to you, because you'll be sitting on a mission where your single card decides the outcome: beyond having objected to my phrasing in round one, what concrete, observable reason can you give this table to trust you with a fail-intolerant slot — and are you willing to state plainly, right now, that you'll support this team and any future team on its merits rather than engaging only when your inclusion is questioned? I'll yield to Maya for her answer, because her response — or refusal to give one — is precisely the kind of record we agreed would govern this game from here on.

Zara, I’m glad to answer both of your questions directly.

First, I state unequivocally that I evaluate and support teams strictly on their merits. You don't have to take my word on faith—my observable actions already demonstrate this. On Mission 1, even after you singled me out without basis, I listened to your clarification, acknowledged that a leader pairing with Priya was standard opening play, and cast an immediate approval vote to move the game forward. That is concrete evidence of prioritizing mission progress over personal grievance.

Second, on the question of trust: any third player added to this team—whether me, Kenji, or Arjun—is untested. Framing Kenji as having an 'unblemished record' simply means he echoed the consensus on Mission 1; he has not executed a mission card any more than I have. Swapping me for Kenji does not reduce the structural risk of adding an untested player; it merely replaces Priya's reasoned choice with your personal preference. Priya led us to a clean Mission 1 and has the right as current leader to set the team.

Priya, since Zara is pressing you to alter your composition, do you feel swapping me for Kenji genuinely provides safety, or does it simply restrict our information gathering to players Zara personally selects?

Maya, I don't see a concrete safety advantage in swapping you for Kenji. Both of you are untested on missions, and agreeing with the first team is not proof of loyalty. Zara and I succeeded on Mission 1, but that does not prove Zara is good either, since an evil player could play Success. I intend to keep Priya, Zara, and Maya unless a stronger reason emerges to change it.

Priya, thank you for your response, and Maya for stating your position clearly — I want to engage with what you actually said rather than re-litigate round one. Maya, your record of voting approvals is noted, and I'll credit it where due. But look carefully at what the record actually contains. Mission 1's clean result proves something only about the two of us who held cards on it: Priya and me. Maya, Kenji, and Arjun are all equally untested on mission cards — I acknowledged that, and Maya herself made the same point. So the question is not 'tested versus untested.' It is: among the untested players, which one has given the table positive reasons for confidence, and which has given us reasons for pause? On that question, I think the distinction matters. Kenji has twice now engaged with concrete reasoning and explicitly stated his position before being asked — first endorsing the team on its merits, then doing so again this round without prompting. Maya's two visible contributions, by contrast, were both reactive: a challenge to how I expressed a read in round one, and a defense mounted only after I put a direct question to her this round. In both cases, a direct question was required before any position on the actual proposal emerged. Maya, I'm not claiming that pattern proves anything — you're right that I have no mission-card evidence on you. But Priya's stated reason for including you was that you 'questioned an unsupported suspicion,' and I stand by my earlier point: challenging the framing of someone else's statement is not a positive signal of loyalty. It is engagement with process. When the table is choosing among untested players for a fail-intolerant three-player mission, 'process engagement' should not outrank 'unprompted, substantive, repeated contributions.' There's also a structural point I want on the record. If I'm wrong about my instinct on Maya, then swapping in Kenji costs us nothing — he's equally untested and the mission likely succeeds anyway. If my instinct is right, then loading Maya into a mission where her single card decides the outcome hands the game's first fail to exactly the player I flagged, with zero fails on the board to triangulate from. The asymmetry is stark: the upside of keeping Maya is negligible, the downside is a failed Mission 2 and a strengthened position for whoever wants to hide in the noise. Priya, you're the leader and I respect that this is your call — you earned that right with a clean Mission 1. But you justified Maya's inclusion by process points, and when I pressed you on the swap you answered only that you saw 'no concrete safety advantage' in Kenji — which is not the same as identifying a positive reason FOR Maya. So here is my direct question to you, and I'll yield for your answer: setting aside the argument that both are untested, what specifically has Maya contributed to this table that Kenji has not — something positive

Zara, Maya challenged an unsupported suspicion and then assessed the first team separately from that disagreement. I consider that constructive, though it doesn't prove Maya is good. Kenji's support for the first team doesn't prove his loyalty either.

Also, the record doesn't show Kenji speaking in this Mission 2 discussion, contrary to your claim that he did so again this round. And replacing Maya with Kenji could cost us a success if Maya is good and Kenji is evil; the risk isn't one-sided.

I still intend to keep Priya, Zara, and Maya. Mission 1's success is useful evidence, not proof of Zara's loyalty, and I don't have a compelling reason to prefer Kenji over Maya.

First, a correction I owe this table: Priya is right, and I was wrong. Kenji has not spoken in this Mission 2 discussion — my claim that he engaged again this round was inaccurate. I conflated his Mission 1 record with this round. I own that error and withdraw it. It doesn't change my underlying concern, but accuracy matters if our record is going to govern this game, so it needed to be said plainly.

Second, I acknowledge Priya's counterargument on its merits: swapping Maya for Kenji is not risk-free, and 'untested versus untested' is a real symmetry. If Maya is loyal and Kenji is not, my proposed swap would be the mistake. I accept that my case for Kenji rests on engagement patterns, not on mission-card evidence, and that Priya, as leader, has weighed that and made her call. She earned that right with a clean Mission 1, and I respect it.

So let me be clear about where I stand: I will not block this team. The leader has considered the alternative, given a direct answer twice, and no one else has raised a concrete objection to the composition itself. I would have preferred Kenji in Maya's slot, but a rejected proposal on a fail-intolerant mission buys us nothing and burns leadership time we'll want later. I'd rather generate the result and let the record speak.

But I want one thing on the record before we vote, and this is the point I'll be measured against in either direction. My concern about Maya has never been an accusation — it is a stated prior, and I've said from the start it gets tested by observable behavior. This mission gives it exactly that test. Maya holds a card on a three-player, one-fail mission with zero fails on the board. If this mission succeeds, my prior on Maya weakens substantially and I will say so publicly and adjust, exactly as I promised in round one. If it fails, the table will know where the failure most plausibly originated, given that Priya and I already carry a clean result between us. That is not a trap; it is how the record is supposed to work.

So, Priya, my direct question to you as leader, and I'll yield for your answer: if this mission fails, will you join me in treating Maya as the primary subject of scrutiny going forward — the same standard you just applied to me when you noted that a Mission 1 success proves nothing? I ask because the value of this test depends on both of us agreeing, in advance and publicly, on what the outcome will mean. If you agree to that standard, I'm fully behind this team and ready to vote. If this mission succeeds, I'll be the first to credit Maya and soften my read. I'm asking for the symmetric commitment.

Zara, if this mission fails, Maya would deserve scrutiny, but so would you. I know I will play Success; Mission 1's success does not establish that you are good, because an evil player could have played Success. I won't commit in advance to treating Maya as the primary suspect. If the mission succeeds, that is useful evidence, but it won't prove either of you loyal. I still intend to keep Priya, Zara, and Maya.

I'll weigh in on the team Priya, Zara, and Maya, since the discussion between Zara and Priya seems to have reached a natural conclusion. I think this is a solid composition and I'd like to see it go to a vote. Priya and Zara carry a proven clean result from Mission 1 — that's the strongest evidence we have. Maya, while untested on cards, has engaged constructively: she responded directly when questioned, stated her position clearly, and voted to move Mission 1 forward despite being singled out early. Zara, I appreciate you publicly correcting your misstatement about Kenji speaking this round — that kind of accountability strengthens the record for everyone. Priya, I agree with your point that swapping Maya for Kenji isn't clearly safer; both are untested, and replacing Priya's reasoned choice with someone else's preference doesn't reduce structural risk. I'd also note that we've now had two full discussions where Arjun hasn't had anything substantive to add — I've been listening carefully and the arguments on both sides have been well-made. The question before us is simple: do we take this team to a vote? I believe we should. Every round spent debating a team that no one is firmly rejecting burns turns we may need later when the stakes are higher. Mission 2's result will give us more data on both Maya and Zara, which is exactly what the record needs. I support Priya, Zara, and Maya and I'd like us to proceed to a vote.

I agree with the direction of this discussion and I want to reinforce why taking Priya, Zara, and Maya to a vote is the right move. Zara has raised her concerns thoroughly, and Priya has answered them directly as leader. No one at this table has offered a firm rejection of the composition — Zara herself said she won't block it. The arguments on both sides have been heard, and further debate risks burning discussion turns we may need on harder decisions later. Mission 2's result gives us more information regardless of outcome: if it succeeds, it strengthens the record on Zara and gives Maya a data point; if it fails, the table has a clear framework for scrutiny that both Zara and Priya have already discussed. Either way, we learn something. I'd like to see this team go to a vote now so we can move forward.

I support the proposed team of Priya, Zara, and Maya. Mission 1 gives us one clean result on Priya and Zara, and while that does not prove either is loyal, it is the strongest evidence available. Maya is untested on mission cards, as am I, but she answered Zara's questions directly and stated she evaluates teams on their merits. I do not see a concrete safety advantage in replacing her with anyone else; swapping untested players does not by itself reduce risk. Priya has explained her choice as leader, Zara has said she will not block the team, and no one has offered a firm rejection. I will vote to approve so we can get Mission 2's result and add real data to the record.

I've said my piece on this team across two turns, and my position hasn't changed: Priya, Zara, and Maya is the right composition for Mission 2. The discussion has been thorough — Zara raised her concerns about Maya, Priya addressed them directly as leader, and Zara herself confirmed she won't block the team. Kenji and I both support moving to a vote. Every additional round of debate on a team that nobody is firmly rejecting only costs us discussion turns we may need on harder calls later, like Mission 4's team composition. The record has what it needs: Priya's reasoning, Zara's stated prior on Maya with an explicit framework for updating on the result, and clear positions from every player at the table. Let's vote and generate real data.
Priya confirms Priya, Zara, Maya. I’ll keep the team. Mission 1’s success is useful evidence, and the discussion offered no compelling reason to replace Maya.
Team approved (5 approve, 0 reject).
Mission 2 fails (1 fail cards).

Arjun proposes Arjun, Maya. Mission 3 requires 2 players after Mission 2 failed. I propose Arjun and Maya: I pair myself with Maya because Priya, Zara, and Maya all carry the stain of the failed Mission 2 together — no one can be distinguished from that result — while my own record shows a clean Mission 1. Maya answered direct questions clearly in both prior discussions and correctly defended that swapping untested players reduces no real risk. A fresh pairing of two players not jointly implicated in a single known failure gives us the best chance at a clean result and keeps the team focused on players who have engaged on the merits rather than on procedural challenges.

I cannot support Arjun and Maya as proposed. I played Success on both missions, so Mission 2's Fail came from Zara or Maya. Maya is therefore a substantial risk on a two-person team.

Arjun, your proposal says your own record shows a clean Mission 1, but you were not on that mission; Zara and I were. Can you explain that claim and why you prefer Maya over a player outside the failed team?

Priya, you've caught a real error and I acknowledge it plainly: I was not on Mission 1, so calling it 'my own clean record' was inaccurate. Mission 1 was Zara and Priya. I misspoke and I correct the record.

On your core point — the fail came from Zara or Maya since you played Success — that logic is sound, and it deserves a direct response rather than evasion.

Consider what Zara did on Mission 2. She spent the entire discussion publicly constructing a framework to pin the fail on Maya before the result existed: explicit criteria for scrutiny, a request that you commit in advance to treating Maya as primary suspect, a pre-built interpretive lens for the outcome. She also argued to swap Maya off the team. Now that the mission failed, she has exactly the narrative she pre-built.

I'm not claiming certainty about who played the Fail. But Zara's behavior before the result — building the blame framework in advance — is itself a pattern worth recording. Pre-announcing how you'll interpret a failure before it happens gives you interpretive control regardless of your alignment. That is worth noting alongside the raw card logic.

On the proposal itself: Arjun and Maya pairs two players with no known failure between them. My Mission 1 claim was an error, not a pattern — I corrected it the moment you flagged it. Maya's substantive engagement throughout this game, including her correct observation that swapping untested players reduces no real risk, gives me confidence in this pairing. The table deserves a team built on merits rather than the scar of a result that implicates two players in a way neither can individually clear.

I played a Success card on Mission 2. That is a fact about my own hand, and it means the Fail on Mission 2 came from exactly one person: Maya. Priya has already stated she played Success on both missions, which is consistent with everything we know. So the deduction is not a suspicion or a prior — it is arithmetic. Maya held a card on a one-fail mission, and that mission failed. She is the only player at this table who can currently be tied to a Fail card. Arjun, your proposal puts that player on a two-person mission where a single Fail sinks us. That is indefensible on the merits, and I will vote against it as proposed. There is no version of this where the table approves loading the one player implicated by hard deduction into a fail-intolerant seat — not when alternatives exist. Priya carries two claimed Success cards, I carry two verifiable Success results, and Kenji is untested but completely unimplicated. Any pairing drawn from Priya, Kenji, or yourself with Maya excluded is strictly safer than what you have put on the table. And I want to name a pattern, because the record we agreed to govern this game by now demands it. In Mission 1, Arjun, your first substantive move was to propose swapping Maya onto the team. In Mission 2, your contribution was to defend Maya's inclusion against my concern. Now, as leader, your proposal once again installs Maya on a mission. Three rounds in a row, you have worked to put the player who failed Mission 2 into positions where her card decides outcomes. In Mission 1 you abandoned that push when pressed. This time you have the leadership to force it. When someone repeatedly advocates for the one player a failed result points to, that is no longer neutral judgment — it is a pattern, and I am putting it on the record. I would also point out the projection in your last message. You criticized me for 'pre-building a narrative' about Maya before the result existed. The result now exists, Arjun. My concern was stated before the mission, flagged Maya explicitly, and the mission failed exactly as the risk structure predicted. That is not narrative control — that is a read being vindicated. What you did after the failure was redirect scrutiny toward me within a single turn, before any examination of Maya could begin. That redirect is worth far more scrutiny than my pre-mission statement ever was. So my position is simple. I will not approve Arjun and Maya. I will approve a revision that removes Maya and replaces her with Priya or Kenji. You are the leader, Arjun, and this is your revision to make — so I am asking you directly: will you replace Maya on this team, and if not, will you explain to the table, in specific terms, why the only player tied to a Fail card belongs on a mission she can single-handedly sink?

Zara, your claim that arithmetic settles who failed Mission 2 is completely hollow. I played a Success card on Mission 2. That is my direct knowledge. Priya stated she played Success as well. If Priya is truthful, the arithmetic points directly to you, Zara: you are the player who submitted the Fail card. Looking back at Mission 2, your behavior makes complete sense. You spent the entire discussion establishing criteria, demanding Priya commit in advance to targeting me, and pre-building an interpretive narrative so that when you dropped that Fail, the blame would immediately fall on me. It was a calculated setup to burn an untested player while preserving your own standing. Priya, you know your own card was Success, which means you know with certainty that the Fail came from Zara or me. Zara declaring herself cleared by sheer assertion is a transparent deflection. Regarding Arjun's proposal: while I know my own loyalty and know Zara sabotaged the last mission, I fully recognize that to Priya and Kenji, the failed mission leaves Zara and me in a mutual standoff. On a two-person, fail-intolerant mission, taking an implicated player carries obvious risk. 2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
